# <a href="https://lhdjung.github.io/scrutiny/"><img src="man/figures/logo.png" align="left" height="150" alt="scrutiny website" /></a> scrutiny

scrutiny tests published summary statistics for consistency using techniques like GRIM, GRIMMER, and DEBIT. It makes these methods easy to use in a tidyverse-friendly way, hoping to help forensic meta-science go mainstream.

You can use the most important parts in the [Error detection](https://errors.shinyapps.io/scrutiny) Shiny app instead.

Besides ready-made tests, scrutiny has a system for implementing new consistency tests, duplicate analysis, and data wrangling helpers. See the [articles](https://lhdjung.github.io/scrutiny/articles/) for details.

Install the package from CRAN:

```{r warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("scrutiny")
```

Alternatively, install the development version from GitHub:

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
remotes::install_github("lhdjung/scrutiny")
```

## Get started

GRIM-test all values in a data frame with `grim_map()`. The `consistency` column says whether each mean (`x`) is consistent with its sample size (`n`).

```{r example}
library(scrutiny)

# Example data:
pigs1

# GRIM-testing for data frames:
grim_map(pigs1, digits_x = 2, items_averaged = 1)
```

Test percentages instead of means:

```{r}
pigs2

grim_map(pigs2, digits_x = 1, items_averaged = 1, percent = TRUE)
```

Choose how the means were rounded --- below, up from 5. The plot adjusts to the rounding method. Blue tiles are consistent, red tiles inconsistent:

```{r}
pigs1 |>
  grim_map(rounding = "up", digits_x = 2, items_averaged = 1) |>
  grim_plot_grid()
```

Use DEBIT to test means and standard deviations of binary data:

```{r}
pigs3

pigs3 |>
  debit_map(digits_x = 2, digits_sd = 2)

pigs3 |>
  debit_map(digits_x = 2, digits_sd = 2) |>
  debit_plot()
```

## Guiding ideas

> (...) a critical inspection of the published literature should not be mischaracterized as a hobby for the overly cynical, nor as so-called "methodological terrorism". On the contrary, carefully evaluating presented data is a cornerstone of scientific investigation, and it is only logical to apply this also to the published literature. If we are not willing to critically assess published studies, we also cannot guarantee their veracity.

--- van der Zee et al. (2017, pp. 8-9)

> (...) data thugs (...) demand data and if they do not receive it, they contact editors and universities and threaten to write blogs and tweets about the errors uncovered.

--- Eric A. Stewart (six retractions; quoted in Pickett 2020, p. 178)

## AI usage since 1.0.0

Almost all scrutiny code before version 1.0.0 was written by me. No version before 0.6.0 contained any appreciable amount of AI-generated code. The first CRAN version, 0.2.2, was released even before ChatGPT was.

However, version 1.0.0 brought vast improvements largely because I used LLMs (mostly Claude) to write most of the new code. Not only did this fix many bugs, iron out API quirks, enable new features, and improve performance, but it also made testing in scrutiny much more thorough. Unit tests are now dramatically more comprehensive than they used to be, with grid sweeps that test key functions over entire ranges of systematically constructed inputs. This has increased my confidence that the code is correct.

I loved maintaining scrutiny as a hand-crafted passion project, but LLMs now write code well enough that refusing to use them would have been a huge missed opportunity. Even the Linux kernel [allows for AI usage](https://docs.kernel.org/process/coding-assistants.html) now, so I am in good company.

## References

Pickett, J. T. (2020). The Stewart Retractions: A Quantitative and Qualitative Analysis. *Econ Journal Watch*, *17*(1), 152--190. <https://econjwatch.org/articles/the-stewart-retractions-a-quantitative-and-qualitative-analysis>.

van der Zee, T., Anaya, J., & Brown, N. J. L. (2017). Statistical heartburn: An attempt to digest four pizza publications from the Cornell Food and Brand Lab. *BMC Nutrition*, *3*(1), 54. <https://doi.org/10.1186/s40795-017-0167-x>.
